prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "ServiceNow, Inc." (ticker NOW). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:

   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?

   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?

   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?

   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?

   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?

   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?

   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: ServiceNow fits several Rule Breaker traits: it leads IT service management with about 44% share, has a strong platform advantage (98% renewal rate) and a CEO with a clear AI vision, and analysts debate its valuation. It misses on consumer brand recognition and on recent momentum, since the shares are about 30% below their level a year ago after the 2026 software selloff.
summaries.buffett: ServiceNow has a durable franchise with high switching costs, growing free cash flow ($4.6 billion in 2025) and no dividend-paying track record to judge. A Buffett-style investor would likely balk at the price (about 89 times trailing GAAP earnings), the $2 billion a year of stock compensation and the 2026 shift to debt-funded acquisitions such as the $7.75 billion Armis deal.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the lock-in of a system of record used by about 90% of the Fortune 500 and its high gross margins. Inverting, the main ways it could fail are AI agents bypassing workflow software and acquisition integration missteps, and the price leaves little margin for error.
summaries.lynch: ServiceNow is a clear fast grower (revenue up 21-31% a year since 2020) with a simple story: more companies run more work and AI agents on its platform. The trailing P/E of about 89 is far above its growth rate, though the forward non-GAAP P/E near 35 with roughly 20% EPS growth is closer to Lynch's comfort zone.
summaries.fisher: ServiceNow scores well on Fisher's points: a large market runway, steady new products (Now Assist AI crossed $1 billion in annual contract value in 2026), heavy R&D ($2.96 billion in 2025) that produces results, and a strong sales organisation. Weaker points are shrinking GAAP margins in 2026 and the dilution from stock compensation.
summaries.graham: ServiceNow fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it pays no dividend, had GAAP net losses as recently as 2018, and trades at about 89 times trailing earnings and over 11 times book value. It passes only on size and financial strength.
summaries.thiel: ServiceNow started with a dominant share of a small niche (IT help-desk ticketing) and expanded into HR, customer service, security and AI governance, a textbook Thiel path. Its technology is better but not ten times better than rivals, and its future depends on owning the 'AI Control Tower' layer before model makers or Microsoft do.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's focus on Rule-of-40 efficiency and AI winners fits ServiceNow well: revenue growth of about 24% plus a free-cash-flow margin above 30% gives a Rule of 55+. After a 2026 drawdown of about 60% from the high, the question he would ask is whether AI expands or shrinks seat-based software spending.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for earnings acceleration and price momentum; ServiceNow offers raised 2026 guidance and a strong rebound from the $81 low in June 2026, but the stock is still down about 30% over 12 months and GAAP earnings fell in H1 2026. It is more a contested recovery than a clear momentum leader.
summaries.smith: ServiceNow looks like a Terry Smith 'good company': high gross margins (about 78% in 2025), strong cash conversion and a long growth runway with limited capital needs. The concerns are the high valuation on GAAP earnings, large stock compensation and the recent turn to debt-funded M&A, which lowers returns on capital.
summaries.greenblatt: ServiceNow does poorly on the Magic Formula: GAAP operating income of about $1.7 billion over the last twelve months is only about 1% of its roughly $149 billion enterprise value. Its return on tangible capital is high, but the earnings yield is far too low.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool, ServiceNow has an extraordinary business (switching costs, 98% renewals) and capable management, and it reinvests cash into R&D, buybacks and acquisitions. The third leg, reinvestment at high returns, is less certain after paying about $10 billion for Moveworks, Armis and Veza.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bargains at deep discounts; ServiceNow is a high-quality but richly valued growth stock. Even after its 2026 fall it trades well above a conservative DCF value, so it does not fit 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much'.
summaries.wood: ServiceNow is a beneficiary of enterprise AI agents, which fits ARK's AI platform theme, and its AI annual contract value passed $1 billion in 2026. ARK tends to favour more disruptive, earlier-stage companies, and ServiceNow could itself be disrupted by AI-native agents.
summaries.ackman: ServiceNow matches several Ackman criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with a dominant market position and high barriers to entry. Its rising leverage ($7.5 billion of debt) and the valuation are the main issues he would weigh.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model fits only partly: ServiceNow's scale lets it outspend rivals on R&D, but it does not pass savings to customers through lower prices, instead raising prices with premium AI tiers. Its long runway and owner-like CEO purchase ($3 million in February 2026) are positives.
summaries.valentine: Valentine's test of a huge, painful problem and a big market is met: large organisations need to coordinate IT, HR and service work, and ServiceNow targets $30 billion of subscription revenue by 2030. It is a mature, public company rather than the early-stage venture Valentine backed.
summaries.nash: On Tom Nash's process, ServiceNow passes on secular trend, revenue growth (24% in Q2 2026), Rule of 40 and moat, scoring about 80 of 130 on the 13 categories. It fails several instant-kill tests: debt ($7.5 billion) now exceeds cash and short-term investments ($4.7 billion), GAAP operating margin is below 20%, and Nash's DCF at 12% gives about $107 a share, below the $142 price.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $141.97 on October 16, 2026, up about 40% from about $100 in late April 2026 and 75% above its June low of $81.24, but about 33% below its 52-week high of $211.48.

g4.evidence: CEO Bill McDermott (former SAP CEO) leads it, institutions own about 87% of shares, and partners include Microsoft, NVIDIA and Accenture.

g6.evidence: Some commentators flag the trailing P/E of about 89, but after the 2026 selloff many analysts call it cheap, with 36 of 42 rating it Buy (MarketBeat, October 2026).

simple.evidence: It sells subscriptions (97% of 2025 revenue) to software that tracks and automates IT, HR and customer-service requests, which a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue has grown at least 20% every year from 2020 ($4.52B) to 2025 ($13.28B), and operating cash flow rose every year from $1.79B to $5.44B.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is clear and the CEO bought $3.0 million of stock in February 2026, but pay relies heavily on stock awards ($1.96 billion of stock compensation in 2025) and McDermott is both chairman and CEO.

b6.evidence: It mostly builds on one platform, but it spent about $10 billion on Moveworks, Armis ($7.75 billion) and Veza in 2025-2026, which some see as following peers into security and AI agents.

roic.evidence: Returns were high and debt-free before 2026, but trailing GAAP net income of about $1.67 billion on roughly $13 billion of net invested capital (about 12-13%) is moderate after the debt-funded Armis deal.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 operating cash flow of $5.44 billion minus $0.87 billion of capex gave about $4.58 billion of free cash flow, 2.6 times GAAP net income of $1.75 billion.

b10.evidence: It retains all earnings, but the share price ($141.97) is about the same as five years ago on a split-adjusted basis, so market value per share has barely grown despite cumulative earnings.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF (31.9% FCF margin, 22% growth for 5 years, 12% discount, 4% terminal growth) gives about $107 a share, below the $141.97 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 35 times 2026 non-GAAP EPS estimates ($4.07) and a 3.1% free-cash-flow yield with 22% revenue growth, the price is reasonable for quality, but high on GAAP earnings (about 89 times).

mu5.evidence: Its 98% renewal rate and $29 billion RPO make sudden failure unlikely, but AI agents bypassing seat-based workflow software and acquisition integration are real ways it could weaken.

reinvest.evidence: Management targets $30 billion of subscription revenue by 2030 (about 19% a year), funded by R&D of nearly $3 billion a year at roughly 80% subscription gross margins.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower: subscription revenue rose 24.5% in Q2 2026, and the story is simple, more workflows and AI agents on one platform.

ly3.evidence: The trailing GAAP P/E is about 89 versus 2026 non-GAAP EPS growth of about 16% (consensus $4.07).

runway.evidence: It is expanding from IT into HR, customer service/CRM, security (Armis) and AI governance, with 37% of revenue outside North America in 2025.

ly7.evidence: The CEO bought about $3.0 million of shares in February 2026 and the company repurchased $2.2 billion in H1 2026, but diluted shares rose from 1,012 million (2020) to 1,047 million (2025) and other insiders sold small amounts in August 2026.

ly8.evidence: It is widely covered (about 49 analysts) and well known among investors as a large-cap software leader.

fi2.evidence: As ITSM matured it added HR, customer service, App Engine and Now Assist AI agents, and launched the AI Control Tower in 2025-2026.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $2.96 billion in 2025 produced products like Now Assist, which passed $1 billion in annual contract value in 2026.

fi4.evidence: It closed 244 deals over $1 million in net new ACV in Q4 2025 and had 658 customers above $5 million ACV in Q2 2026, up about 23%.

longterm.evidence: It spends about 22% of revenue on R&D and paid about $10 billion for acquisitions in 2025-2026 despite near-term GAAP margin pressure.

gr1.evidence: It had $13.3 billion of 2025 revenue and a market value of about $147 billion, and is in the Fortune 500 for the fourth year.

ni10.evidence: It reported GAAP net losses in 2016 ($414 million), 2017 ($117 million) and 2018 ($27 million) before turning profitable.

gr4.evidence: ServiceNow has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a loss of $2.52 in 2016 (pre-split) to a profit of $1.67 in 2025 (post-split), far more than a one-third gain.

gr6.evidence: The price of $141.97 is about 90 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of about $1.57.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 89 times price/book of about 11.7 (market cap about $147 billion vs equity of $12.5 billion) is about 1,000, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its platform is the market leader with about 44% ITSM share, but it is not ten times better than Atlassian, BMC or Microsoft tools.

timing.evidence: Enterprises are deploying AI agents now, and Now Assist annual contract value rose from $600 million at end-2025 to over $1 billion in 2026.

th3.evidence: It began by dominating IT help-desk ticketing and expanded into HR, customer service, security and AI governance, targeting $30 billion of subscription revenue by 2030.

team.evidence: CEO Bill McDermott ran SAP for nearly a decade, and since he joined in 2019 ServiceNow revenue has nearly tripled.

th5.evidence: It has a direct enterprise sales force plus partners such as Accenture and Deloitte, reaching about 90% of the Fortune 500.

durable.evidence: Deep integration as a system of record should endure, but AI agents could change how enterprise software is bought within 10-20 years.

pa4.evidence: Strong recurring revenue (98% renewal, $29 billion RPO) limits business risk, but a valuation premium and new debt mean meaningful price-loss risk.
